 What Is Qi2.2 Wireless Charging? A Detailed Breakdown
 To understand Qi2.2, it helps to see how the standard evolved. The Wireless Power Consortium (WPC) introduced the original Qi standard in 2010, establishing a universal foundation for wireless charging. Qi2 arrived in 2023, integrating magnetic alignment technology (Magnetic Power Profile, or MPP) to ensure perfect device-to-charger positioning. Now, Qi2.2—officially released by the WPC in Spring 2025—raises the power ceiling from 15W to 25W and introduces strict thermal requirements.

 How Does Qi2.2 Deliver 25W Wireless Charging?
 Hitting 25W wirelessly isn't just about cranking up the power—it requires a tightly integrated system of hardware and software working in perfect sync. Here's how Qi2.2 actually makes it happen.
 MPP 2.0: Precision That Prevents Waste
 The secret to Qi2.2's speed lies in its Magnetic Power Profile (MPP) 2.0 system. While earlier wireless pads required careful positioning to avoid energy loss, Qi2.2 uses a ring of magnets that snap your iPhone into the exact optimal position—with ±0.5 mm precision.
 This isn't just about convenience—it's about efficiency. When the coils are perfectly aligned, less energy dissipates as heat and more flows directly into your battery. At 25W, even a slight misalignment would cause significant power loss and overheating.
 EDC: The Smart Negotiator
 Extended Data Communication (EDC) is the brain behind the operation. It enables real-time dialogue between your iPhone and the charger, dynamically negotiating voltage and current based on battery level and thermal conditions.
 This isn't a one-size-fits-all handshake—it's a continuous conversation that adjusts power delivery second by second. By enabling real-time thermal monitoring and precise foreign object detection, EDC dynamically regulates power delivery to prevent overheating, ensuring safe and reliable 25W charging at all times.
 The Thermal Challenge—and Why Active Cooling Matters
 At 25W, electromagnetic coil energy loss generates significant heat. Here's the physics problem: electromagnetic coil losses generate heat roughly proportional to the square of the current. Jumping from 15W to 25W doesn't just produce 67% more heat—it can more than double it.
 Without active cooling, the charger's internal temperature would spike, forcing the system to throttle power back to 15W or lower within minutes. That's why Qi2.2 mandates a strict 40°C surface temperature limit—and why the best chargers integrate fans or thermoelectric cooling to sustain full 25W output without compromising safety or battery health.
 That's why the best Qi2.2 wireless chargers integrate built-in fans or thermoelectric cooling systems to sustain peak performance.
 For a deeper dive into what makes a Qi2 charger truly fast, check out our detailed guide: What Makes a Qi2 Wireless Charger Truly Fast for iPhone 17 ?
 What Does Qi2.2 Mean for iPhone 17?
 The iPhone 17, 17 Pro, and 17 Pro Max all support Qi2.2 25W wireless charging out of the box. In real-world testing, a Qi2.2 25W charger can push an iPhone 17 Pro from 0% to 50% in approximately 22 minutes. Measured data indicates that actual charging power can reach nearly 30W on the iPhone 17 Pro without a case—more than 10W higher than what a Qi2.0 charger delivers under the same conditions.
 With iOS 26, all iPhone 16 and iPhone 17 models (excluding the 16e) unlock full Qi2 25W support. For iPhone 17 Air, speeds max out at 20W.
 For iPhone 17 users, this translates to effortless, "drop-and-go" charging that actually hits the ultra-fast 25W speeds.
 Qi2.2 vs MagSafe: What iPhone 17 Users Need to Know
 With both standards now capable of 25W, iPhone 17 users face a genuine choice. Here's how they actually compare.
 Different Origins, Same Result. MagSafe is Apple's proprietary system, built around its own certification program (Made for MagSafe). Qi2.2, by contrast, is an open industry standard developed by the Wireless Power Consortium. For iPhone 17 users, the practical outcome is identical: 25W wireless charging on the 17, 17 Pro, and 17 Pro Max. The difference lies not in speed, but in ecosystem and flexibility.
 Magnet Compatibility Is Fully Interchangeable. Both standards use the same 44-mm magnet ring specification. A Qi2.2 charger snaps onto an iPhone with the same satisfying click as a MagSafe charger—and vice versa. This means you can mix and match accessories without worrying about physical fit.
 Where They Diverge: Ecosystem and Price. MagSafe chargers undergo Apple's strict certification process, which often commands a premium price. Qi2.2 chargers deliver the same magnetic alignment and charging speed but benefit from broader competition across multiple brands, typically at lower price points. Additionally, Qi2.2 chargers work seamlessly with Android devices that support the standard—something MagSafe cannot claim.
 If you're all-in on Apple and prefer first-party polish, MagSafe is a reliable route. But for most iPhone 17 users, Qi2.2 offers the same core experience with greater versatility and better value—especially when building out a multi-device charging setup across home, car, and travel.

 Whether at home, in the car, or on the go, the right Qi2.2 wireless charging solution makes all the difference. Here are our top picks—each with active cooling and precise magnetic alignment to keep your iPhone 17 charging at full 25W speed.

Its 45W USB-C port can even charge a MacBook Air. Thanks to SnapCool active cooling, you can charge two devices simultaneously via wireless and wired outputs without any throttling—a unique advantage over competitors.

 The Anker Prime Wireless Charging Station (3-in-1, MagGo, AirCool, Foldable) folds completely flat for easy travel and delivers full 25W Qi2.2 wireless charging, juicing an iPhone 17 Pro to 50% in just 26 minutes. Its AirCool fan reduces heat by 30%, helping maintain stable Qi2 25W charging and preserve battery health. The 3-in-1 design charges your iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods simultaneously, with ActiveShield 5.0 running over 10 million temperature checks daily to protect your devices.
 Best for Road Trip & Daily Commutes:
 For iPhone 17 users who need fast charging on the road, the Anker Prime Wireless Car Charger (MagGo, AirCool, Pad) is the fastest wireless car charger for iPhones available. It delivers 25W Qi2.2 wireless charging, pushing your iPhone 17 to 50% in just 22 minutes. The locking adjustable clamp and ultra-strong magnetic attachment keep your phone secure even on bumpy roads—tested across eight rugged conditions.
 Conclusion
 Qi2.2 wireless charging represents a genuine breakthrough for iPhone 17 users. With 25W speeds, precision magnetic alignment, and mandatory active cooling, it finally delivers the fast, reliable wireless charging experience that users have been waiting for. Whether you’re at your desk or on the road, Qi2.2 chargers like Anker MagGo 2 Pro Magnetic Power Bank (10K, Qi2 25W, Active Cooling) make it easier than ever to keep your iPhone 17 powered up—without the cable.
 FAQ
 1. What is the difference between Qi2 and Qi2.2 wireless charging?
 Qi2 supports up to 15W, while Qi2.2 (also known as Qi2 25W) raises the maximum to 25W—about 70% faster. Beyond speed, Qi2.2 enforces a stricter 40°C surface temperature limit and refines magnetic alignment precision to within ±0.5 mm. These improvements ensure safer, more efficient charging, reducing energy waste and heat generation during high-power transfer.
 2. Does the iPhone 17 support Qi2.2 25W wireless charging?
 Yes. All iPhone 17 models—the 17, 17 Pro, and 17 Pro Max—fully support Qi2.2 25W wireless charging. The iPhone 17 Air is capped at 20W. To unlock the full 25W speed, you must update to iOS 26 or later. Also ensure you use a Qi2.2-certified charger; older Qi2 pads will only deliver up to 15W even with the latest software.
 3. Why is active cooling necessary for Qi2.2 25W charging?
 At 25W, coil energy losses generate substantial heat. Without active cooling, chargers would quickly throttle power to avoid overheating, reducing charging speed to much lower levels. Active cooling—using built-in fans or thermoelectric (TEC) systems—dissipates heat continuously, sustaining the full 25W output while keeping your iPhone's battery temperature within safe operating limits for long-term health.
 4. How fast does Qi2.2 25W charge an iPhone 17 Pro?
 A Qi2.2 25W charger can take an iPhone 17 Pro from 0% to 50% in roughly 22 minutes under typical room-temperature conditions without a case. Third-party lab tests have recorded actual power delivery peaking at nearly 30W, which is over 10W higher than what a Qi2 charger achieves in the same scenario—making it nearly as fast as wired charging.
 5. Do I need a special cable or adapter for Qi2.2 25W charging?
 Yes. To hit the full 25W output, you must use a USB-C cable and a power adapter rated at 45W or higher with Power Delivery (PD) support. Using a lower-wattage adapter will limit charging speed. Many premium Qi2.2 products, like those from Anker, include a suitable 45W adapter in the box for convenience.

 What Does Qi2 25W Wireless Charging Mean for Your iPhone 17?
 Qi2.2 is the latest version of the Qi2 wireless charging standard, and it raises the magnetic power profile from 15W to 25W. In plain terms, that means more energy reaches your phone every minute, so top-ups finish noticeably faster.
 With a compatible wireless charging setup, the iPhone 17 Qi2.2 experience looks like this: about 50% charge in roughly 25 minutes, and a quick 10-minute session can get you back to 25%. For context, standard Qi2 15W wireless charging tops out far lower.
 There is a catch, though. Faster wireless charging does not come free — it comes with heat. That is exactly why the Qi2 25W standard pairs higher wattage with a cooling requirement, and why the charger you pick matters as much as the phone you plug it into.
 Why Is Qi2.2 25W So Fast?
 The number on the box is only part of the answer. Qi2.2 25W is fast because several pieces of engineering work together — not because a charger simply cranks up the voltage. Here is what actually changes when wireless charging steps up from 15W to 25W.
 More power per minute. At 25W, the coil pushes roughly two-thirds more energy into the phone than a Qi2 15W charger. That is the single biggest reason top-ups finish faster.
 Higher real-world efficiency. With Magnetic Power Profile precise alignment, less energy is wasted on the way from charger to phone, so a larger share of those 25 watts becomes stored charge instead of warmth.
 Sustained speed, not just a burst. Active cooling keeps the charger from throttling. Without it, 25W is a short sprint before heat forces a slowdown; with a fan, the charger holds full speed for the whole session.
 Smart negotiation. The charger and iPhone talk over the Qi2.2 protocol to settle on the best power level for the connected device, so the phone never pulls more than it can handle.

At 25W, a magnetic charger is pushing nearly 70% more energy through the coil than a Qi2 15W charger, and that surplus shows up as heat on both the charger and the phone.

 What is Qi2.2 25W wireless charging?
 Qi2.2 is the latest version of the Qi2 wireless charging standard, and it raises the magnetic power profile from 15W to 25W. That means a compatible charger can deliver more energy per minute to your phone, cutting top-up times noticeably compared with Qi2 15W or standard Qi charging. The 25W tier also pairs higher wattage with effective cooling to manage the extra heat.
 Does 25W wireless charging damage the iPhone 17 battery?

The Qi2.2 25W standard is designed around thermal management for this reason.  iPhone 17 May Support Qi 2.2, Capable of Up to 25W Wireless Charging
 Thursday June 5, 2025 2:54 am PDT by Tim Hardwick 
 Apple appears to be moving to the next-generation Qi 2.2 wireless charging standard, according to regulatory filings on Taiwan's NCC certification website. Qi2.2 is the forthcoming update to the Wireless Power Consortium's (WPC) Qi standard, building on improvements introduced with Qi 2.1.
Spotted by 91mobiles.com , the filings reveal two new MagSafe charger models – A3503 and A3502 – that support the upgraded Qi 2.2 standard. The chargers feature the familiar white puck design with braided cables in 2-meter and 1-meter lengths, respectively. 
 It's a notable upgrade mainly because of the faster charging speed. Qi 2.2 is technically capable of up to 25W charging output. In contrast, the Qi 2 standard maxes out at 15W (although iPhone 16 models support upgraded MagSafe charging – with a 30W Apple charger, the iPhones can charge at up to 25W ). The WPC has since released the Qi 2.1 standard, but no Apple devices officially support it.
 Testing documents show the chargers work with devices ranging from the iPhone 16 back to the iPhone 11, indicating the Qi 2.2 pucks will have broad compatibility with existing devices, but charging speeds are going to be limited when using older models. Devices looking to take advantage of the faster charging speeds will need a corresponding advanced charging chip, similar to Samsung's Power Management Integrated Circuit (PMIC) . 
In addition to faster charging, Qi 2.2 offers improved magnetic alignment and charging efficiency compared to its predecessor. The standard also features backward compatibility with older Qi chargers.
 Apple has not officially announced these new chargers, but their appearance in Taiwan's regulatory databases indicates we're likely to see a public release in the coming months. It also increases the likelihood that the upcoming iPhone 17 models will support the new charging standard – but that doesn't guarantee they will charge at the maximum 25W. Apple is expected to announce the iPhone 17 lineup around September, while the broader industry is expected to launch Qi 2.2-compatible phones, chargers, and accessories later this year.
 Editor's note: This article originally reported that Qi 2.2 offers a maximum charging output of 50W, which turned out to be based on false information. We apologize for the error.

Qi2 vs. MagSafe: Which wireless charger is best for your iPhone? | Macworld 
 When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn't affect our editorial independence .
 by Simon Jary 
 Contributor, Macworld 
 Updated 
 Qi2 vs. MagSafe: Which wireless charger is best for your iPhone?
 Updated 
 Oct 21, 2026 
 Summary created by Smart Answers AI 
 In summary:
 Macworld compares Qi2 and MagSafe wireless charging standards, explaining how both support up to 15W for iPhone 12 through 15, while newer iPhone 16 models can reach 25W via the latest Qi2.2 standard.
 Qi2 chargers match MagSafe speeds without expensive Apple certification fees, making them a more affordable option with broad compatibility across iPhone and Android devices.
 Matching your iPhone model to the correct charger standard appears essential for achieving maximum wireless charging efficiency.
 Not having to find the right cable or carry one around with you makes wireless charging a convenient way of charging your mobile devices—iPhone, Apple Watch, AirPods and many third-party gadgets.
 There are multiple wireless charging standards and technologies. Here we will explain the major ones— Qi , MagSafe , Qi2 and the latest Qi2 25W (aka Qi2.2 ). Knowing which is which will help you to make your charging life more efficient. Here we look at Qi2 vs MagSafe and Qi2 25W vs Qi2 and Apple’s updated 2024 version of MagSafe. Which is best for your model of iPhone?
 It’s a little more nuanced, but in general, iPhones 16, 17 and 18 (and the iPhone Duo) should now charge wirelessly at up to 25W with supporting certified Qi 2.2 chargers. Older iPhones are limited to the 15W maximum if they support certified Apple MagSafe or Qi2. Chargers that are merely “MagSafe Compatible” are usually limited to 7.5W wireless charging. Note that the iPhone Air is limited to 20W wireless, the 16e to 7.5W and 17e to 15W.
 iPhone wireless charging speeds in brief: 
 iPhone 8-11 series and 16e: Qi 7.5W . 0-50% in around 90 minutes.
 iPhone 12-15 series and 17e: MagSafe 15W and Qi2 15W . 0-50% in around 45 minutes.
 iPhone Air: 20W Qi2 . 0-50% in around 40 minutes.
 iPhone 16 and 16 Pro: MagSafe 22W and Qi2.2 22W . 0-50% in around 35 minutes.
 iPhone 16 Plus, 17, 17/18 Pro, 16/17/18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo: MagSafe 25W and Qi2.2 25W . 0-50% in around 30 minutes.
 Don’t worry too much about the difference between 22W and 25W—the charging time difference will be marginal given environmental conditions such as room temperature will also make an impact.
 How does wireless charging work?
 Wireless charging uses electromagnetic induction to power your devices. The charging pad and your phone both include copper wire coils. Plug the pad into a power source and the charger’s coil generates a magnetic field. When you place your phone onto the charging pad, the phone’s coil converts that magnetic field into an electric current, thus charging the phone.
 Apple pioneered improved magnetic connection between charger and phone with MagSafe, and it’s mainly the tighter magnetic fit that drives faster and faster wireless charging.
 What is Qi2? 
 Qi2—supported by the iPhone 12 and up—speeds up wireless charging from 7.5W to 15W and makes chargers cheaper as well as more efficient. It is very like MagSafe, which is unsurprising as Apple allowed the Wireless Power Consortium (WPC) to use MagSafe as the basis of Qi2.
 In short, Qi2 brings the magnetic benefits of MagSafe, but also make third-party iPhone chargers faster and potentially cheaper. Manufacturers are more likely to create new products when the market is larger (iPhone and Android) and costs should come down, too.
 Apple’s latest version of its iPhone MagSafe Charger can wirelessly charge the iPhone 16 series at 22-25W. Older iPhones can use this charger but at a 15W maximum as before. Qi2 took its time catching up, but it has now: keep reading.
 We have tested Qi2 chargers vs chargers certified as MagSafe by Apple, and can confirm that 15W Qi2 charges supporting devices at an equivalent speed to 15W MagSafe, and much faster than merely MagSafe-compatible 7.5W chargers. More details of our wireless charging speed tests below.
 Belkin first announced two Qi2 magnetic wireless charging devices in September 2023. Belkin
 What is Qi2.2 25W?
 The latest Qi2 25W standard (officially Qi 2.2) matches Apple’s 25W wireless charging speed. We have tested many 25W chargers, including the Belkin 25W UltraCharge Pro 3-in-1 Magnetic Charging Dock , Ugreen MagFlow Power Bank , 25W Baseus PicoGo AM52 Power Bank and ESR’s 25W CryoBoost 3-in-1 Charging Station among others.
 Samsung waited until its Galaxy S26 Ultra to jump on the fast magnetic wireless charging bandwagon with Qi2 25W, and Google was first out of the Android blocks with Qi2 25W compatibility with its Pixel 10 Pro XL . The lesser Google Pixel 10 Pro is pegged back at 15W Qi2. Google calls its version of Qi2 “PixelSnap”.
 Wireless charging from Qi to Qi2.2
 First, let’s look at the original Qi, which all iPhones post iPhone 8 support.
 Foundry
 What is Qi wireless charging?
 Qi is a Chinese word that means “energy flow”. Pronounced “chee”, Qi is the basic and most popular wireless charging standard, launched in 2008 but not seen on an iPhone until 2017’s iPhone 8.
 Note that plain Qi2 has little magnetic connection between phone and charger so is less efficient at transferring power as more is wasted depending on the placement of the phone on the charger. Better magnetic attachment and therefore faster charging arrived with MagSafe and Qi2.
 Apple continues to support the Qi wireless charging standard with its most recent iPhones—and the iPhone 12 and later models are compatible with Qi2, more on which later. This means that iPhones from the iPhone 8 onwards can be placed on a Qi-compatible charger to start charging without a cable. (Of course, the Qi charging pad or stand itself has to be connected via a cable to a power charger.)
 While wireless charging means less wear and tear to your devices, it is not as efficient as charging via a cable (wired charging) as some of the energy is lost between the charging pad and the device placed on it.
 Qi users will know that you have to ensure your device is placed in exactly the right alignment for fast wireless charging to take place. Place the iPhone on the pad incorrectly and you end up either charging much more slowly or not at all. Many of us have dropped a phone on a Qi charger only to find out later that it wasn’t in the right place and so annoyingly never started charging—a problem largely solved by Apple’s MagSafe.
 While Qi’s maximum wireless charge is 15W, Apple’s iPhone supports only 7.5W via Qi.
 Which iPhones use Qi? 
 Qi charging is built into the iPhone 8, X, XR, XS, SE, 11, 12, 13, and 14 families. The iPhone 15/16/17/18 and Air/Duo work with Qi but are rated as Qi2; see later. The outlier is the curious iPhone 16e that goes all the way back to plain old Qi; the 17e is fine.
 Foundry
 What is MagSafe wireless charging?
 Apple’s magnetic MagSafe iPhones contain a ring of magnets built around its Qi charging coil. As a result, you can magnetically clamp charging accessories onto the iPhone. In fact, you can magnetically attach non-charging accessories, such as wallets and mounts, too.
 MagSafe—from 2020’s iPhone 12 on—makes missing the charging pad’s coils much less likely with its ring of magnets quickly finding the charging alignment sweet spot—on a compatible charger—so you will always connect and less energy is wasted.
 Magnetic Power Profile (MPP) technology uses magnets to perfectly align the coils of the wireless charging transmitter and receiver before transferring power.
 iPhones can work with wireless chargers that are either MagSafe certified by Apple (“made for MagSafe”) or are compatible with MagSafe—plus less sophisticated Qi chargers.
 Certified MagSafe chargers can supply up to 25W to the iPhone, while merely MagSafe compatible chargers are limited to 7.5W , but compatible chargers are usually cheaper. That 25W charging speed is currently limited to the iPhone 16 and 17 ranges and Apple’s own MagSafe Charger . iPhones 12/13/14/15 max out at 15W using MagSafe. The iPhone Air won’t charge faster than 20W wirelessly. In fact, the iPhone 16 and 16 Pro are pegged back at 22W, while the larger 16 Plus and 16 Pro Max support the while 25W. The 16e is out of the picture at just 7.5W and the 17e makes it to 15W. 
 (Note that the iPhone 12 mini only charges at 12W with MagSafe.)
 We have tested the best MagSafe chargers for iPhones and the best MagSafe power banks for iPhones. This reviews roundup now also includes 15W Qi2 and 25W Qi2.2 chargers as they arrive to market.
 Some thicker cases get in the way of MagSafe wireless charging so make sure your iPhone’s case is MagSafe compatible—see our roundup of the best iPhone 15 Cases , best iPhone 16 cases , best iPhone 17 cases and best iPhone 18 cases .
 Wireless charging is great, but it’s not as fast as wired charging. For truly fast iPhone charging, use a cable connected to at least a 20W USB-C charger. For the iPhone 15 and later that means a USB-C to USB-C cable ; for older iPhones you’ll need a USB-C to Lightning cable . A USB-A to Lightning cable won’t offer iPhone fast charging. Click here for more iPhone fast-charging tips .
 Somewhat confusingly, MagSafe is also the name for Apple’s wired-charging standard for its MacBooks—connecting the charging cable to the MacBook’s MagSafe port via magnets, meaning it is not only easy to connect but, if accidentally disconnected, it pops out rather than dragging your laptop to the floor. This version of MagSafe is magnetic and safe and has a charging connection for MacBooks but is not wireless. We explain the difference between MagSafe on Mac and MagSafe on iPhones in our Complete guide to Apple MagSafe: What is MagSafe? 
 Which iPhones use MagSafe? 
 MagSafe wireless charging is built into the iPhone 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, and 18 families, with the exception of the 16e. It’s also supported by the iPhone Air and iPhone Duo.
 Foundry
 What is Qi2 wireless charging?
 Qi2 (“chee too”) is the latest version of the Qi “energy flow” wireless charging standard, and it’s supported by all iPhones from the iPhone 12.
 Famed for its “Not Invented Here” strategy, Apple can be quite precious about adopting other technical standards. It has a long history of rejecting any idea that didn’t originate within Apple itself. However, thankfully Apple has cooperated with the creation of Qi2 to the extent that in effect it gave the Wireless Power Consortium (WPC) MagSafe to use as the basis for Qi2’s Magnetic Power Profile that defines how the new generation Qi works. Apple is a WPC “steering member” and chair of the board of directors.
 So what is Qi2 and why is it so great?
 Think of Qi2 as not just MagSafe for Android, but MagSafe benefits for all compatible wireless charging products.
 Qi2 means chargers won’t have to be certified by Apple to support 15W charging. They should, however, meet the technical demands of the WPC. In short, a Qi2 charger will deliver twice as fast charging as “MagSafe-compatible” chargers.
 As MagSafe certification costs manufacturers a fee to Apple, removing this should result in cheaper chargers that match Apple-certified chargers in terms of speed. 
 Which iPhones use Qi2? 
 Qi2 wireless charging works with all iPhones 12. and onwards, except the 16e.
 Simon Jary / Foundry
 What is Qi2 25W wireless charging?
 Qi2 25W is the latest version of the Qi “energy flow” wireless charging standard. Its technical name is Qi2.2.
 It started rolling out in wireless charging products from the mid-2025 and is now seen in many new wireless charging products.
 So what is Qi2 25W and why is it so great?
 Qi2 25W means chargers can support up to 25W wireless charging. They have to meet the technical demands of the WPC. In short, a Qi2 25W charger will deliver 10W more power than Qi2 and 3.3 times as fast charging as MagSafe-compatible chargers.
 The use of a Magnetic Power Profile (MPP) provides better alignment but also reduces magnetic field leakage caused by misalignment. This minimizes the build-up of heat and ensures optimal charging efficiency. A ±0.5mm magnetic alignment precision improves charging efficiency by “up to 40%”, according to manufacturer Baseus.
 Qi2 25W products also feature next-generation thermal regulation with stricter 40°C surface limits and enhanced coil layouts. This ensures that less energy is wasted and provides 15% better charging efficiency—even in motion or with slight misalignment.
 Which iPhones use Qi2 25W?
 Qi2 25W wireless charging will work with the iPhone 16 family and later (except the 16e and 17e). The iPhone Air supports Qi2 25W but only up to 20W, which is likely caused by the super-thin phone’s thermal management. The iPhone 16 and 16 Pro can make it to only 22W according to Apple. The iPhone Duo does support 25W Qi2.2.
 For Qi2 25W to work at full 25W supporting iPhones must have installed at least iOS 26 or later.
 Which is best MagSafe, Qi2 or Qi2 25W?
 First, MagSafe, Qi2 and Qi2 25W are all better than plain Qi. Owing in large part to their magnetic connection, they are more efficient and definitely offer faster wireless charging than Qi.
 For all extents and purposes, Qi2 looks pretty identical to MagSafe so iPhone 12/13/14/15 users can choose between MagSafe or Qi2 without fear. iPhone 16/17/18/Air/Duo owners, however, should look to MagSafe or Qi2 25W, as Apple’s own MagSafe Charger and soon Qi2 25W chargers can reach charging speeds of up to 25W when paired with the latest range of iPhones.
 All should clamp chargers magnetically to the iPhone in the same way and allow for between 15W and 25W wireless charging.
 Will Qi2 chargers work with MagSafe?
 Although technically very similar, Apple is likely to still require MagSafe certification for non-Qi2 products to reach 15W wireless charging. Both the charger and the device must be certified for Qi2 for it to work at 15W, in the same way as MagSafe. However, it is likely that future MagSafe-certified products will also be certified for Qi2, and post iOS 17.2 all iPhones (except 16e) will work natively with Qi2 and Qi2.2 chargers.
 For consumers it’s a win-win as Qi2 and Qi2 25W means faster wireless charging will be brought to more devices and people. For product marketers it may be a bit of a labelling nightmare until all the chargeable devices catch up with the technology: expect MagSafe Compatible (7.5W), MagSafe (15W or 25W), Qi2 15W (15W) and Qi2 25W or Qi2.2 (25W).
 Is Qi2 as fast at wireless charging as MagSafe?
 As the Wireless Power Consortium used Apple technology to build the Qi2 specification, it is true that Qi2 matches MagSafe for speed. Both can charge at up to 15W and use the largely same magnetic attachment tech. Note the 25W charging potential of the Apple MagSafe Charger and iPhone 16/17, plus the same charging speed from Qi2 25W.
 The first Qi2 charger we tested and reviewed at Macworld was the Anker MagGo 3-in-1 Wireless Charging Station . We tested its Qi2 wireless charging speed by charging an iPhone 15 Pro all the way to a 100% full charge, and taking timings at 30%, 50% and 80%. We did the same using a Apple’s own MagSafe Charger and also via a straight wired USB-C connection.
 The fastest way to charge an iPhone is via a wired connection: USB-C to Lightning for iPhones older than the iPhone 15, and USB-C to USB-C for the iPhone 15 and later. The average wired-charging time in our tests was 25 minutes to 50%, 55 minutes to 80% and 70 minutes to 100%.
 Our wireless charging tests for officially Apple-certified MagSafe chargers (using Apple’s own Wireless Charger) and for Qi2 magnetic wireless charging (using the Anker MagGo) had remarkably similar timings. There was some variance either way but also small differences using the same charger so we are confident that using these two magentic wireless charging technologies came up with the same basic results on average: 45 minutes to 50%, 90 minutes to 80% and 115 minutes to 100%. 
 In summary, then, MagSafe and Qi2 charging at 15W results in the same times and so can be considered equal—except for the 25W MagSafe potential of the iPhone 16/17–and the same from Qi2 25W now it is released. And, again as expected, merely MagSafe-compatible chargers took twice as long as the 15W chargers: 45 minutes to 30%, and 90 minutes to 50%.
 Our tests demonstate that Qi2 25W will charges an iPhone 16 Pro from 0–50% in just over 30 minutes—manufacturers often claim 25 minutes but that is under clinical conditions. In Macworld’s real-world tests 32-34 minutes is the average. In comparison, a Qi2 15W charger generally takes about 45 minutes to reach the same level—this would work out as the 25W option being around 45% faster than the 15W chargers. Wireless charging depends on many factors, such as device settings, usage during charging, and ambient temperature.
 Don’t concern yourself greatly about the 22W limit of the iPhone 16 and 16 Pro. The 3% difference between that and 25W is marginal.
 Why does phone charging speed slow down as the battery gets fuller?
 Batteries charge slower the fuller they get, especially in the last 10–20% of charging. The fuller the battery is, the slower it absorbs energy.
 To start with, a Lithium-Ion battery accepts whatever current it can, but as the battery gets closer to being full it accepts less current, and so the power being transferred tapers off.
 Imagine you were filling up a glass with water. You can start with the faucet or tap at full blast, but as the glass gets fuller, you have to slow the flow down to avoid the water spilling over, until eventually just a trickle of water goes in as you try to get it right up to the brim.
 If the battery didn’t charge this way and instead filled up at full blast till reaching 100%, it would get very hot and you’d risk damaging it to the point it might explode!
 Slowing down the charge when the battery is getting closer to full also increases the number of charge cycles a battery can go through before it permanently loses capacity.
 Taking advantage of this, if you need to charge quickly, stop at 80%, use the device for a while and then top back up to 80% before the charging speed starts to slow.

Qi2.2 Wireless Charging Speed by Phone: 16 Models Measured 
 Skip to content 
 As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. All test results and recommendations are based on independent engineer measurements — not affiliate relationships. 
 A Qi2.2 charger is sold as 25W, and nothing on the box tells you whether your phone will use it. Compatibility lists online group the Galaxy S25 and S26 series, the Pixel 10 line and the iPhone 17 line together as Qi2.2 phones. So this page puts every  Qi2.2 wireless charging speed  I have measured into one table: 16 phones, the same classes of pad, with and without a case, each row linked to the full test it came from.
 The bench does not agree with the lists. On  seven of the sixteen phones , a Qi2.2 pad measured no faster than a Qi2.0 one, because those phones never used the faster tier. And on every Galaxy, the magnetic case decided more than the pad did: bare on an ordinary Qi2.2 pad they read between  9.89W  and  11.91W , and with a magnetic case the fastest of them reached  32.10W .
 Every figure here is the power drawn at the wireless charger’s input, the only place a meter can sit in a wireless setup, so it runs higher than what reaches the battery. That is explained below, along with why the eye-catching readings from actively cooled pads are kept out of the main table.
 Of 13 phones I measured on both a Qi2.2 and a Qi2.0 pad at the charger input, six drew more power on Qi2.2 (the iPhone 17 Pro, Galaxy S26 Ultra, Galaxy S26+, Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra and Pixel 10 Pro XL) and seven did not: the Galaxy S26, Galaxy S25 Ultra, Z Flip 8, Z Fold 7, Z Flip 7, Pixel 10 and Pixel 10 Pro.
 Table of Contents

 Qi2.2 Wireless Charging Speed at a Glance 
 Highest readings:  Galaxy S26 Ultra  32.10W  (2mm magnetic case), Pixel 10 Pro XL  31.67W  (no case), iPhone 17  30.88W  (2.13mm case).
 Faster on Qi2.2 than on Qi2.0 (6):  iPhone 17 Pro, Galaxy S26 Ultra, Galaxy S26+, Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra, Pixel 10 Pro XL.
 No faster (7):  Galaxy S26, Galaxy S25 Ultra, Z Flip 8, Z Fold 7, Z Flip 7, Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro.
 Measured on Qi2.2 only (3):  iPhone 17, iPhone 17 Pro Max, iPhone Air.
 Galaxy phones need the case.  None has built-in magnets. Bare on an ordinary Qi2.2 pad, every one I measured read between 9.89W and 11.91W, and Samsung’s own SFWC charger beat that on every Galaxy I tested both ways.
 A thick case can cost almost nothing or 18.42W , and on the same phone, which one you get depends on the pad.
 ⚠ These are  charger-input watts , not battery watts, and they cannot be compared with wired figures.
 Qi2.2 Wireless Charging Speed by Phone: The Full Table 
 Each row is one phone. The Qi2.2 and Qi2.0 readings in a row come from the same test session and the same case condition, so they can be compared directly. Where two Qi2.2 readings are shown, two different Qi2.2 pads were tested; the higher one is in bold.

 How to read this table.  Treat it as groups, not a ranking. Readings were taken in the low-battery window where a phone accepts peak power, and the starting percentage was never identical between runs, so a difference of a fraction of a watt (20.53W against 20.55W on the Galaxy S26) is measurement conditions, not hardware. The gap that is real is the one between groups:  25.77W to 32.10W  on the phones where Qi2.2 engaged, and  18.58W to 21.14W  on either pad for the phones where it did not.
 The “No” phones fall short for two different reasons. The Galaxy S26, S25 Ultra, Z Flip 8, Z Fold 7 and Z Flip 7 negotiated Qi2.0 even on the Qi2.2 pad. The Pixel 10 and Pixel 10 Pro ran the Qi2.2 pad on a 9V rail ( 8.85V  on the Pixel 10), just as a Qi2.0 pad does; only the Pro XL moved it to  14.87V .
 On a Qi2.2 pad, phones that used the faster tier drew 25.77W to 32.10W at the charger input, while the Galaxy S26, S25 Ultra, Z Flip 8, Z Fold 7, Z Flip 7, Pixel 10 and Pixel 10 Pro stayed between 18.58W and 21.14W on either a Qi2.2 or a Qi2.0 pad.
 What This Means for the Pad You Buy 
 Find your phone in the table. One of three answers applies.
 If your phone is in the “Yes” group, a Qi2.2 pad is worth paying for 
 On these six phones the tier is the difference. The iPhone 17 Pro read  29.92W  on a Qi2.2 pad against  19.16W  on a Qi2.0 pad in the same condition; the Z Fold 8 read  25.77W  against  19.47W . What to look for in a listing is the certification, Qi2.2 (often sold as “Qi2 25W”), rather than a wattage number on its own.
 On the four Galaxy phones in this group, the pad only pays off with a magnetic case the phone can detect. Bare, the Z Fold 8 read  10.36W  on the same Qi2.2 pad that gave it 25.77W with the case.

 On the six phones that gained from Qi2.2, a Qi2.2 pad drew 25.77W to 32.10W in my tests, against no more than 21.51W on a Qi2.0 pad. This charger is Qi2.2-certified, so it sits in the class I measured. On a Galaxy it still needs a magnetic case to reach that tier.

 If your phone is in the “No” group, a Qi2.0 pad is the whole answer 
 On these seven, a Qi2.2 pad and a Qi2.0 pad landed in the same band. The Z Flip 8 drew  20.53W  on Qi2.2 and  21.14W  on Qi2.0; the Pixel 10 drew  18.85W  and  19.14W . A more expensive pad buys nothing on these phones, so a certified Qi2.0 (Qi2 15W) pad is the ceiling worth paying for. The Galaxy phones in this group still need a magnetic case for any Qi2 pad, or the Samsung option below.

 If you own a Galaxy and don’t want a magnetic case 
 Use Samsung’s own fast wireless charger, which needs no magnet at all. The Galaxy section further down shows how far ahead of a bare Qi2.2 pad it landed on every Galaxy I tested.
 Case Thickness: Same Phone, Same Pad, Only the Case Changed 
 Every row below changes one thing, the case, and keeps the phone and the pad fixed. This is the question behind most “wireless charging through a case” searches: how much power does a phone case actually cost?
 Phone · pad Thinner case Thicker case What happened Full test

 Pixel 10 Pro XL · first Qi2.2 pad 31.67W (no case) 29.63W  (3mm) Held on Pixel 10 Pro XL Qi2 charger test 
 Pixel 10 Pro XL · second Qi2.2 pad 30.95W (2mm) 19.53W  (3mm) Fell back to Qi2.0 Pixel 10 Pro XL Qi2 charger test 
 A thicker case does one of two things, and the meter shows which. Either the pad keeps the rail it negotiated and simply pushes less current (the iPhone 17 Pro held  14.95V  while the current fell to  1.34A , and the Z Fold 8 held  15.15V  while it fell to  1.55A ), or the phone drops to a lower protocol, which on the Pixel 10 Pro XL showed up as the pad falling to  8.92V . The first is the gentler outcome on most pads: the Z Fold 8 gave up only a few watts across three cases, though on the iPhone 17 Pro it still took the reading from 30.74W to 20.03W. The second is where the largest loss in this table comes from:  18.42W  on the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s first pad.
 Which of the two you get is decided by the pad as much as the case. The same 3mm case left the S26 Ultra at  22.49W  on one Qi2.2 pad and  11.64W  on another. Pads differ in how much gap between the coils they are built to bridge, none of them print that figure, and a case right at a pad’s limit can make charging start and stop rather than merely slow down. The dependable rule is the thinnest certified case you are willing to live with. A thicker case is not always worse on every pad, either: through a 3.05mm case a Qi2.0 pad gave the iPhone 17 Pro  20.40W , no lower than through a 2.13mm one.
 On a Galaxy S26 Ultra with a 3mm case, one Qi2.2 pad fell back to PPDE at 11.64W while another held Qi2.2 at 22.49W: same phone, same case, measured at the charger input.
 📖 Related Reading Same 3mm case, two Qi2.2 pads: 11.64W on one, 22.49W on the other Which pad tolerates a thick case on the Galaxy S26 Ultra and S26+. 
 If you are choosing a case rather than a pad, the thickness-by-thickness picture is worth seeing on its own.
 📖 Related Reading Wireless charging through a case: a 3mm case took an iPhone 15 Pro from 18W to 9.4W Thickness by thickness, what a case takes off a wireless pad. 
 Galaxy Without a Magnetic Case: Samsung’s Stand Beat a Bare Qi2.2 Pad Every Time 
 No Galaxy phone in this set has magnets of its own. A Qi2 pad decides whether to negotiate Qi2.0 or Qi2.2 only after the phone’s Hall IC detects a magnet ring, so a bare Galaxy never gets that far. It falls back to Samsung’s PPDE mode, a 10W-class tier, and on a pad that does not support PPDE either, all the way down to basic BPP at  7.38W  on the Z Fold 8.

 SFWC is Samsung’s own fast wireless protocol, and it works without a magnet because it does not rely on the magnet handshake at all. It is also Samsung-only: a Samsung SFWC charger gave an iPhone 17 Pro just  11.62W .
 With no case, Samsung’s own 15W SFWC stand gave the Galaxy Z Flip 8 21.44W and the Z Fold 8 18.59W at the charger input, while a Qi2.2 pad gave the same bare phones 10.91W and 10.36W.
 [The gate a bare Galaxy never passes – the Hall IC stays off without a magnet ring and turns on with a Qi2-certified case] 
 If a case is not an option, Samsung’s own charger is the practical route on every Galaxy above.
 ✅ NO CASE NEEDED: 21.44W ON A BARE Z FLIP 8 Samsung 15W Wireless Charger Single (EP-P2400)

 Samsung’s SFWC protocol skips the magnet handshake, so on Samsung’s own 15W charger a bare Z Flip 8 drew 21.44W and a bare Z Fold 8 18.59W, against 10.91W and 10.36W on a bare Qi2.2 pad. This pad runs the same protocol and gave a bare Galaxy S25 Ultra 22.30W. It is for Galaxy phones only.

 On the Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra, though, the no-case route is not the fastest one: a certified case on a Qi2.2 pad still read 25.77W and 26.28W.
 📖 Related Reading Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra wireless chargers: the Qi2.2 pads that reached 26.28W cased Where the faster tier pays off, and which pad to put under a foldable. 
 Why Some Readings Top 25W, and Why Cooled Pads Are Left Out 
 A 25W-class pad reading  30.14W  on an iPhone 17 is not a faulty meter. The meter sits between the wall adapter and the pad, so it counts everything the pad draws: the power sent across the coils plus what the pad and the coils lose as heat along the way. The phone’s battery receives less than the number in the table. That is also why none of these figures can be set against wired numbers, which are measured at the phone’s own port.
 Actively cooled pads are the one kind I keep out of the main table. A pad with a Peltier element and a fan spends part of its input running them; in my Peltier car-mount testing, a reading near 39W can include 9–10W of cooling load. My Galaxy S26 test includes a  38.90W  reading from exactly that kind of pad. It is a real measurement, but it is not comparable with an uncooled pad’s  32.10W , so it is not in the ranking.
 The same caution applies to the foldables. Bare on a cooled Qi2.2 pad they read  17.48W  to  18.40W , which looks like a way around the case, but the phones were still in their PPDE fallback, and part of that figure is the cooler. For a bare Galaxy, the answer is Samsung’s SFWC charger, not a cooled pad.
 One disclosure on those SFWC rows: Samsung’s own SFWC pad lists a built-in cooling fan, so a fan’s draw may sit inside those readings too. They stay in the tables because the gap to a bare Qi2.2 pad is a protocol difference: the stand negotiated SFWC, while the bare phone on the Qi2.2 pad sat in its PPDE fallback.
 Wireless figures on this page are charger-input power: a Qi2.2 pad read 30.14W on an iPhone 17 because the meter counts the pad’s own losses, and a Peltier-cooled pad’s 38.90W on a Galaxy S26 Ultra also includes its cooler and fan.
 The fallback ladder behind every slow reading here (Qi2.2 and Qi2.0, then PPDE, then BPP) is worth ten minutes if the tier names are the confusing part.
 📖 Related Reading PPDE, EPP and Qi2.2 explained: the 10W Samsung tier a bare Galaxy falls back to The fallback ladder behind every slow wireless reading. 
 How These Numbers Were Measured 
 Where the meter sits:  an inline USB-C meter between the wall adapter and the wireless pad, reading voltage, current and power. A wireless link cannot be metered at the phone.
 Battery window:  each reading was taken in the low-battery range where a phone accepts peak power. The exact starting percentage varied, which is why small gaps inside a group are not treated as differences.
 Pads:  listed by certification class: Qi2.2 25W, Qi2.0 15W, and Samsung’s 15W SFWC stand. Where two pads of the same class behaved differently, both are shown.
 Cases:  Qi-certified or magnet-equipped cases, with the thickness given wherever it changed the result.
 Ranges:  the Galaxy S26 series was logged as a range over each run; the table shows the top of each range.
 If you cite these figures,  quote the phone, the pad class and the case condition together. A Qi2.2 reading without its case condition is a different measurement: on the Galaxy S26 Ultra, the same Qi2.2 pad read 10.06W bare and 32.10W with a 2mm case.
 Frequently Asked Questions 
 Which phones get faster wireless charging on a Qi2.2 charger? 
 In my tests, six of the 13 phones I measured on both pad classes: the iPhone 17 Pro, Galaxy S26 Ultra, Galaxy S26+, Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra and Pixel 10 Pro XL. The Galaxy S26, Galaxy S25 Ultra, Z Flip 8, Z Fold 7, Z Flip 7, Pixel 10 and Pixel 10 Pro measured the same on a Qi2.0 pad.
 Do the Galaxy S25 and Galaxy S26 support Qi2.2 wireless charging? 
 Not all of them. The Galaxy S26 Ultra and S26+ did: with a 2mm magnetic case they drew  32.10W  and  27.34W  on a Qi2.2 pad, against  21.51W  and  21.13W  on a Qi2.0 pad. The standard Galaxy S26 negotiated Qi2.0 and read  20.55W , level with Qi2.0. The Galaxy S25 Ultra also fell back to Qi2.0 on a Qi2.2 pad, at  19.67W  against  20.89W  on Qi2.0.
 How fast is Qi2.2 wireless charging on the iPhone 17? 
 With no case on a Qi2.2 pad, the iPhone 17 read  30.14W , the iPhone 17 Pro  29.92W  and the iPhone 17 Pro Max  29.68W  at the charger input. The iPhone Air read  21.95W . A 3.05mm case brought the 17 Pro down to  20.03W .
 Does the Galaxy S26 Ultra need a case for Qi2.2 wireless charging? 
 Yes. It has no magnets, so bare it read  10.01W  and  10.06W  on two different Qi2.2 pads. With a 2mm magnetic case the same two pads reached  30.06W  and  32.10W . A 3mm case split them: one held  22.49W  and the other fell back to  11.64W .
 Is a Qi2.2 charger worth it for the Pixel 10 or Pixel 10 Pro? 
 No. Both ran a Qi2.2 pad on a 9V rail and measured the same as on a Qi2.0 pad:  18.85W  against  19.14W  on the Pixel 10,  19.22W  against  19.50W  on the Pixel 10 Pro. Only the Pixel 10 Pro XL moved up, to  31.67W .
 What is PPDE wireless charging on a Galaxy? 
 PPDE (Proprietary Power Delivery Extension) is Samsung’s own 10W-class wireless mode. It is where a Galaxy lands on a Qi2 pad when no magnet ring is detected: bare on a Qi2.2 pad the Z Fold 8 read  10.36W  in PPDE, against  25.77W  with a magnetic case on the same pad.
 Why did a 25W wireless charger read over 30W on an iPhone 17? 
 Because the reading is taken at the charger’s input, not at the phone: a Qi2.2 pad read  30.14W  on a bare iPhone 17. It includes what the pad and the coils lose as heat, so the battery receives less than the figure shown. On an actively cooled pad, the reading also includes the cooler and fan.
 How much wireless charging power does a phone case cost? 
 Anywhere from almost nothing to  18.42W  in my tests. A 3.05mm case took the iPhone 17 Pro from 30.74W to  20.03W  on a Qi2.2 pad; cases up to 3.6mm cost the Z Fold 8 a few watts while it stayed on Qi2.2; and a 3mm case pushed a Pixel 10 Pro XL down to Qi2.0 at  19.53W  on one pad while another pad held  29.63W . Which result you get depends on the pad.

 The Bottom Line 
 Qi2.2 wireless charging speed  is a property of the phone first and the pad second. Six of the 13 phones I measured both ways got faster on a Qi2.2 pad; seven landed exactly where a cheaper Qi2.0 pad put them. Check your phone’s row before paying for the tier.
 On a Galaxy, the case comes before the pad. Without a magnetic case, no Qi2 pad got a Galaxy past its PPDE fallback, and Samsung’s own SFWC charger is the way to charge one bare.
 And keep the case thin. A thick case costs anything from almost nothing to 18.42W, and which of those you get depends on a pad specification nobody prints. I add new phones to this table as each one goes on the bench.
 📐 Sources & method. Compiled from my own bench tests of 16 retail phones, each linked in the tables above. All wireless figures are charger input power : the meter sits between the wall adapter and the pad, so they include the pad’s own losses and are higher than what reaches the battery; they are not comparable with wired figures measured at a phone’s USB-C port. Actively cooled (Peltier and fan) pads are excluded from the main tables because their readings also include the cooler. Readings were taken in the low-battery window where a phone accepts peak power, and the starting percentage varies between runs, so differences of a fraction of a watt within a group reflect measurement conditions rather than hardware. Pads are identified by certification class. Last updated October 2026. Your results will differ with ambient temperature, case, charger, and starting battery level.

 What is Qi2 wireless charging?
 Qi2 wireless charging is the next generation of the Qi standard, developed by the Wireless Power Consortium.  How Does Qi2 wireless charging work? 
 Qi wireless charging uses electromagnetic induction between two coils -- one in the charging pad and one in the device -- to transfer power wirelessly. The pad generates a magnetic field when powered, which induces a current in the device's coil, charging its battery. The charging itself works without magnets (just slower and less convenient), but the magnetic alignment is what makes the experience so seamless—especially for those pulling their phone out of a bag for quick top-ups.
 Is Qi2 better than MagSafe?
 Not necessarily—it depends on what you need. MagSafe offers tight integration with Apple devices and accessories, while Qi2 is an open standard that gives consumers more third-party options. For older MagSafe-compatible iPhones, Qi2 can provide a similar magnetic charging experience at up to 15W. Qi2.2 goes further by supporting up to 25W on compatible devices, making it more compelling for newer iPhones. If you're looking for a versatile magnetic power bank that works across ecosystems, explore the Qi2 Power Banks .
 What is Qi2.2 25W, and is it different from Qi2?
 Yes. Qi2.2 is the newer version of the Qi2 standard, commercially referred to as Qi2 25W. Original Qi2 supports magnetic wireless charging up to 15W, while Qi2.2 raises the maximum power transfer to 25W and introduces improvements to power control, magnetic loss management, and foreign-object detection at higher power levels. However, not every Qi2 accessory supports Qi2.2 25W, so check the product certification before buying.
 Does Qi2.2 wireless charging make an iPhone hotter?
 Higher charging power can increase thermal demands, but wattage alone does not determine how hot a phone becomes. Charging efficiency, coil alignment, ambient temperature, case thickness, and thermal management all affect heat. For frequent charging, particularly when your power bank stays attached while you use the phone, choose products with effective active cooling technology and temperature monitoring rather than focusing only on the 25W figure.

 Does iPhone 17 Have MagSafe?
 If you've followed iPhones over the past few years, the answer to " Will iPhone 17 have MagSafe? " won't surprise you Every model in the iPhone 17 lineup, including the 17, 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max, and the new ultra-thin iPhone Air, comes with MagSafe built in.
 Apple first rolled out MagSafe in 2020 with the iPhone 12 series, and it's been part of every flagship iPhone since (except the iPhone 16e). Where things do differ is speed:
 iPhone 17 / 17 Pro / 17 Pro Max: up to 25W over MagSafe. With a 30W or higher USB-C adapter, you can reach about 50% in roughly 30 minutes using an iPhone 17 MagSafe charger.
 iPhone Air: up to 20W over MagSafe.
 Compared with the iPhone 16 lineup, MagSafe speeds stay about the same. But if you're upgrading from an older iPhone 12-15 model, which maxes out at 15W , the jump to 25W is easy to notice. It means faster top-ups and shorter waits, especially when your battery is low.
 The iPhone 17 Air MagSafe charging speed is a bit slower, capped at 20W.
 How Does MagSafe Work on iPhone 17?
 MagSafe on the iPhone 17 works the same way it has since its debut, but now with higher power limits. At a simple level, MagSafe uses a ring of magnets surrounding the Qi wireless charging coil . When the phone gets close to a MagSafe charger, the magnets pull it into the ideal position. That alignment helps the charger deliver power more efficiently.
 When MagSafe first launched with the iPhone 12, the cap was 15W , already faster than the 7.5W that older Qi chargers delivered. That stayed true across iPhone 12, 13, 14, and 15. The iPhone 16 series (2024) bumped the limit to 25W , and the iPhone 17 family keeps that same ceiling.
 Here's what charging with MagSafe on an iPhone 17 looks like:
 Plug your MagSafe charger into a USB-C PD power adapter. For the quickest results, use at least a 30W adapter.
 Place the back of your iPhone 17 against the charger puck. You'll feel the magnetic snap as the coils align .
 A quick animation and chime confirm everything is connected.
 From there, iOS adjusts the power flow automatically. It monitors temperature, battery level, background tasks, and settings like Optimized Battery Charging. You don't need to do anything; your phone manages the whole process to protect battery health.
 But MagSafe is more than a wireless charging aid . The same magnets support a wide range of accessories . Cases, wallets, battery packs, and car mounts all snap into place and stay secure. On iPhone 17, the system works as you would expect. You get wireless convenience plus a library of magnetic add-ons.
 What About Qi2 25W?
 You've probably also heard about the Qi2 25W wireless charging , standard for the iPhone 17. This is the big update for wireless charging this year.
 Qi2 takes the same core idea as MagSafe: magnets for alignment + faster wireless charging speeds .
 It's an open standard developed by the Wireless Power Consortium , which means more certified third-party chargers from trusted brands, not only Apple's puck.
 When Qi2 arrived in 2023, it offered up to 15W for MagSafe-enabled iPhones. With the Qi2 latest update, certified chargers can now reach 25W on the iPhone 17 lineup. That matches Apple's own second-generation MagSafe speeds, so you can hit about 50% in ~30 minutes with the right charger.

 Easy alignment : The magnets do the work. You drop your phone onto the MagSafe charger , and it snaps into place without you fussing over position.

 Good everyday speed : Getting to 50% in about 30 minutes wirelessly is quick enough for most people.
 Cons 
 Full speed requires newer hardware : Only Apple's newer MagSafe chargers (and a 30W+ adapter) can deliver the full 25W.
 Usually more expensive : Official MagSafe accessories cost more than many Qi2 alternatives.
 Less efficient than wired : Wireless charging always uses more energy and creates more heat than a cable.

 Qi2 25W Wireless Charging: Pros and Cons
 Qi2 is the open standard inspired by MagSafe's magnetic idea. With the Qi2 update, it now reaches 25W on iPhone 17 models, matching MagSafe's top speed.
 Pros 
 More choice : Because Qi2 is an open standard, lots of reputable brands offer certified magnetic wireless chargers in different sizes, colors, and prices.
 Same 25W speeds as MagSafe : A Qi2 25W-certified charger can hit the same "50% in about 30 minutes" milestones.
 Backwards compatible : Qi2 chargers still work with older Qi and Qi2 phones.
 Often more affordable : Many Qi2 chargers cost less than Apple's official MagSafe puck.
 Cons 
 Look for Qi2 specifically : Many Qi2 chargers on the market are still limited to 15W. You need "Qi2 25W" for full speed.
 Quality varies : Magnet strength and cooling design differ from brand to brand. Cheap options may feel weaker or run warmer.
 Want the fastest wireless charging speed possible? The Anker Prime Wireless Charging Station is built for that.

 USB-C Wired Charging: Pros and Cons
 USB-C is still the fastest way to fill an iPhone 17 battery. With a 40W or higher USB-C PD adapter , you can reach about 50% in roughly 20 minutes .
 Pros 
 Fastest option by far : When your battery is low, nothing beats wired charging.
 More efficient and cooler : Less wasted power and less heat compared with wireless charging.
 Works everywhere : You can plug into laptops, power banks, car chargers, and public ports.
 Lower cost : A good cable and a standard USB-C charger are often cheaper than buying a wireless stand.
 Cons 
 Less convenient : Plugging in and unplugging is a small chore compared with snapping onto magnets.
 Slight wear over time : Using a port repeatedly adds minor wear to cables and connectors.
 No clean "floating stand" setup : If you enjoy the tidy look of a magnetic stand, a cable won't match that.

 Conclusion
 Choosing how to charge your iPhone 17 is easier once you understand how iPhone 17 MagSafe compares with Qi2 and USB-C. MagSafe gives you quick, reliable wireless charging with that familiar magnetic snap. Qi2 opens the door to more charger styles and matching 25W speeds. USB-C still wins when you need the fastest top-up. Most people use a mix of all three, depending on the moment. With the right setup, your iPhone 17 stays ready whenever you are.

 What to do if MagSafe stops working on iPhone 17
 If MagSafe stops working on your iPhone 17, first remove any thick, metal, or magnetic case, wallet, or grip and try charging with the phone bare. Make sure you're using an official MagSafe or Qi2-certified charger and a compatible USB-C power adapter plugged directly into the wall. Clean the back of your phone and the charger, restart your iPhone, and test with a different power adapter or outlet to rule out a weak power source. If it still doesn't work, reach out to Apple Support.
 Which iPhone supports MagSafe?
 MagSafe works on every iPhone starting with the iPhone 12 series and continuing through the iPhone 17 lineup (except the iPhone 16e). All of these models include a built-in magnetic ring that helps the charger lock into place for more reliable wireless charging. Older iPhones with Qi charging , like the iPhone 8 through iPhone 11, can still charge on a MagSafe puck, but they won't snap on and charge more slowly.
 Is MagSafe better than wireless charging?
 MagSafe is wireless charging, but with a helpful twist. The magnets center your phone on the charger, so it loses less energy and charges more consistently. You'll also see faster speeds on supported iPhones compared with regular Qi pads. The main downsides are cost and compatibility, since MagSafe accessories tend to be pricier and work best with Apple devices. Standard Qi and Qi2 chargers are more universal and easier on your budget.

 Which magnetic wireless speed is my iPhone? Wireless charging speeds compared
 Tuesday March 3, 2026. 10:18 AM , from Macworld Reviews 
Macworld
Not having to find the right cable or carry one around with you makes wireless charging a convenient way of charging your mobile devices—iPhone, Apple Watch, AirPods and many third-party gadgets.
There are multiple wireless charging standards and technologies. Here we will explain the major ones—Qi, MagSafe, Qi2 and the latest Qi2 25W. Knowing which is which will help you to make your charging life more efficient. Here we look at Qi2 vs MagSafe and Qi2 25W vs Qi2 and Apple’s updated 2024 version of MagSafe. Which is best for your model of iPhone?
It’s a litle more nuanced, but in general, iPhones 16 and 17 should now charge wirelessly at up to 25W with supporting certified Qi 2.2 chargers. Older iPhones are limited to the 15W maximum if they support certified Apple MagSafe or Qi2. Chargers that are merely “MagSafe Compatible” are usually limited to 7.5W wireless charging. Note that the iPhone Air is limited to 20W wireless, the 16e to 7.5W and 17e to 15W.
iPhone wireless charging speeds in brief:
iPhone 8-11 series and 16e: Qi 7.5W. 0-50% in around 90 minutes.
iPhone 12-15 series and 17e: MagSafe 15W and Qi2 15W. 0-50% in around 45 minutes.
iPhone Air: 20W Qi2. 0-50% in around 40 minutes.
iPhone 16 and 16 Pro: MagSafe 22W and Qi2.2 22W. 0-50% in around 35 minutes.
iPhone 16 Plus, 16 Pro Max, 17, 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max: MagSafe 25W and Qi2.2 25W. 0-50% in around 30 minutes.
Don’t worry too much about the difference between 22W and 25W—the charging time difference will be marginal given environmental conditions such as room temperature will also make an impact.
How does wireless charging work?
Wireless charging uses electromagnetic induction to power your devices. The charging pad and your phone both include copper wire coils. Plug the pad into a power source and the charger’s coil generates a magnetic field. When you place your phone onto the charging pad, the phone’s coil converts that magnetic field into an electric current, thus charging the phone.
Apple pioneered improved magnetic connection between charger and phone with MagSafe, and it’s mainly the tighter magnetic fit that drives faster and faster wireless charging.
What is Qi2? 
Qi2, supported by the iPhone 15, 16 and 17 families (except 16e) at launch and the iPhone 13 and iPhone 14 as of iOS 17.2, speeds up wireless charging from 7.5W to 15W and makes chargers cheaper as well as more efficient. It is very like MagSafe, which is unsurprising as Apple allowed the Wireless Power Consortium (WPC) to use MagSafe as the basis of Qi2.
In short, Qi2 brings the magnetic benefits of MagSafe, but also make third-party iPhone chargers faster and potentially cheaper. Manufacturers are more likely to create new products when the market is larger (iPhone and Android) and costs should come down, too.
In September 2024, however, Apple announced that the new version of its iPhone MagSafe Charger can wirelessly charge the iPhone 16 series at 22-25W. Older iPhones can use this charger but at a 15W maximum as before. Qi2 took its time catching up, but it has now: keep reading.
We have tested Qi2 chargers vs chargers certified as MagSafe by Apple, and can confirm that 15W Qi2 charges supporting devices at an equivalent speed to 15W MagSafe, and much faster than merely MagSafe-compatible 7.5W chargers. More details of our wireless charging speed tests below.
 Belkin first announced two Qi2 magnetic wireless charging devices in September 2023.Belkin
What is Qi2 25W?
The latest Qi2 25W standard (officially Qi 2.2) matches Apple’s 25W wireless charging speed. We have tested 25W chargers, including the Belkin 25W UltraCharge Pro 3-in-1 Magnetic Charging Dock, Ugreen MagFlow Power Bank, 25W Baseus PicoGo AM52 Power Bank and ESR’s 25W CryoBoost 3-in-1 Charging Station among others.
Samsung waited until its Galaxy S26 Ultra to jump on the fast magnetic wireless charging bandwagon with Qi2 25W, and Google was first out of the Android blocks with Qi2 25W compatibility with its Pixel 10 Pro XL. The lesser Google Pixel 10 Pro is pegged back at 15W Qi2. Google calls its version of Qi2 “PixelSnap”.
Wireless charging from Qi to Qi2.2
First, let’s look at the original Qi, which all iPhones post iPhone 8 support.

What is Qi wireless charging?
Qi is a Chinese word that means “energy flow”. Pronounced “chee”, Qi is the basic and most popular wireless charging standard, launched in 2008 but not seen on an iPhone until 2017’s iPhone 8.
Note that plain Qi2 has little magnetic connection between phone and charger so is less efficient at transferring power as more is wasted depending on the placement of the phone on the charger. Better magnetic attachment and therefore faster charging arrived with MagSafe and Qi2.
Apple continues to support the Qi wireless charging standard with its most recent iPhones—and the iPhone 13 and later models are compatible with Qi2, more on which later.
This means that iPhones from the iPhone 8 onwards can be placed on a Qi-compatible charger to start charging without a cable. (Of course, the Qi charging pad or stand itself has to be connected via a cable to a power charger.)
While wireless charging means less wear and tear to your devices, it is not as efficient as charging via a cable (wired charging) as some of the energy is lost between the charging pad and the device placed on it.
Qi users will know that you have to ensure your device is placed in exactly the right alignment for fast wireless charging to take place.
Place the iPhone on the pad incorrectly and you end up either charging much more slowly or not at all.
Many of us have dropped a phone on a Qi charger only to find out later that it wasn’t in the right place and so annoyingly never started charging—a problem largely solved by Apple’s MagSafe.
While Qi’s maximum wireless charge is 15W, Apple’s iPhone supports only 7.5W via Qi.
Which iPhones use Qi? 
Qi charging is built into the iPhone 8, X, XR, XS, SE, 11, 12, 13, and 14 families. The iPhone 15/16/17 work with Qi but are rated as Qi2; see later. The outlier is the curious iPhone 16e that goes all the way back to plain old Qi.

What is MagSafe wireless charging?
Apple’s magnetic MagSafe iPhones contain a ring of magnets built around its Qi charging coil. As a result, you can magnetically clamp charging accessories onto the iPhone. In fact, you can magnetically attach non-charging accessories, such as wallets and mounts, too.
MagSafe—from 2020’s iPhone 12 on—makes missing the charging pad’s coils much less likely with its ring of magnets quickly finding the charging alignment sweet spot—on a compatible charger—so you will always connect and less energy is wasted.
Magnetic Power Profile (MPP) technology uses magnets to perfectly align the coils of the wireless charging transmitter and receiver before transferring power.
iPhones can work with wireless chargers that are either MagSafe certified by Apple (“made for MagSafe”) or are compatible with MagSafe—plus less sophisticated Qi chargers.
Certified MagSafe chargers can supply up to 25W to the iPhone, while merely MagSafe compatible chargers are limited to 7.5W, but compatible chargers are usually cheaper. That 25W charging speed is currently limited to the iPhone 16 and 17 ranges and Apple’s own MagSafe Charger. iPhones 12/13/14/15 max out at 15W using MagSafe. The iPhone Air won’t charge faster than 20W wirelessly. In fact, the iPhone 16 and 16 Pro are pegged back at 22W, while the larger 16 Plus and 16 Pro Max support the while 25W. The 16e is out of the picture at just 7.5W and the 17e makes it to 15W. 
(Note that the iPhone 12 mini only charges at 12W with MagSafe.)

Wireless charging is great, but it’s not as fast as wired charging. For truly fast iPhone charging, use a cable connected to at least a 20W USB-C charger. For the iPhone 15, 16 and 17 that means a USB-C to USB-C cable; for older iPhones you’ll need a USB-C to Lightning cable. A USB-A to Lightning cable won’t offer iPhone fast charging. What is Qi2 wireless charging?
Qi2 (“chee too”) is the latest version of the Qi “energy flow” wireless charging standard.
Famed for its “Not Invented Here” strategy, Apple can be quite precious about adopting other technical standards. It has a long history of rejecting any idea that didn’t originate within Apple itself.
However, thankfully Apple has cooperated with the creation of Qi2 to the extent that in effect it gave the Wireless Power Consortium (WPC) MagSafe to use as the basis for Qi2’s Magnetic Power Profile that defines how the new generation Qi works. Apple is a WPC “steering member” and chair of the board of directors.
So what is Qi2 and why is it so great?
Think of Qi2 as not just MagSafe for Android, but MagSafe benefits for all compatible wireless charging products.
Qi2 will mean chargers won’t have to be certified by Apple to support 15W charging. They should, however, meet the technical demands of the WPC. In short, a Qi2 charger will deliver twice as fast charging as MagSafe-compatible chargers.
As MagSafe certification costs manufacturers a fee to Apple, removing this should result in cheaper chargers that match Apple-certified chargers in terms of speed. 
Which iPhones use Qi2? 
Qi2 wireless charging is built into the iPhone 15, 16 and 17 families (except 16e). As of iOS 17.2, Apple brought the technology to all iPhone 13 and 14 models as well.
While Apple hasn’t stated that Qi2 support will reach the iPhone 12, the first iPhone to support MagSafe, Macworld readers have contacted us to say that Qi2 does indeed work with the iPhone 12 following the release of iOS 17.4. Tested with the Belkin BoostCharge Pro 2-in-1 Magnetic Wireless Charging Pad with Qi2, an iPhone 12 charged up to 15W with the on-screen animation also displayed.

What is Qi2 25W wireless charging?
Qi2 25W is the latest version of the Qi “energy flow” wireless charging standard.
It started rolling out in wireless charging products from the mid-2025 and is now seen in many new wireless charging products.
So what is Qi2 25W and why is it so great?
Qi2 25W means chargers can support up to 25W wireless charging. They have to meet the technical demands of the WPC. In short, a Qi2 25W charger will deliver 10W more power than Qi2 and 3.3 times as fast charging as MagSafe-compatible chargers.
The use of a Magnetic Power Profile (MPP) provides better alignment but also reduces magnetic field leakage caused by misalignment. This minimizes the build-up of heat and ensures optimal charging efficiency. A ±0.5mm magnetic alignment precision improves charging efficiency by “up to 40%”, according to manufacturer Baseus.
Qi2 25W products also feature next-generation thermal regulation with stricter 40°C surface limits and enhanced coil layouts. This ensures that less energy is wasted and provides 15% better charging efficiency—even in motion or with slight misalignment.
Which iPhones use Qi2 25W?
Qi2 25W wireless charging will work with the iPhone 16 family and later (except the 16e and 17e). The iPhone Air supports Qi2 25W but only up to 20W, which is likely caused by the super-thin phone’s thermal management. The iPhone 16 and 16 Pro can make it to only 22W according to Apple,
For Qi2 25W to work at full 25W supporting iPhones must have installed at least iOS 26 or later.
Which is best MagSafe, Qi2 or Qi2 25W?
First, MagSafe, Qi2 and Qi2 25W are all better than plain Qi. Owing in large part to their magnetic connection, they are more efficient and definitely offer faster wireless charging than Qi.
For all extents and purposes, Qi2 looks pretty identical to MagSafe so iPhone 13/14/15 users can choose between MagSafe or Qi2 without fear. iPhone 16 and 17 owners, however, should look to MagSafe or Qi2 25W, as Apple’s own MagSafe Charger and soon Qi2 25W chargers can reach charging speeds of up to 25W when paired with the latest range of iPhones.
The fact that the iPhone 12 isn’t certified as Qi2 compatible demonstrates that Qi2 and MagSafe are not identical.
All should clamp chargers magnetically to the iPhone in the same way and allow for between 15W and 25W wireless charging.
Will Qi2 chargers work with MagSafe?
Although technically very similar, Apple is likely to still require MagSafe certification for non-Qi2 products to reach 15W wireless charging. Both the charger and the device must be certified for Qi2 for it to work at 15W, in the same way as MagSafe. However, it is likely that future MagSafe-certified products will also be certified for Qi2, and post iOS 17.2 all iPhones 13/14/15/16/17 will work natively with Qi2 chargers.
For consumers it’s a win-win as Qi2 and Qi2 25W means faster wireless charging will be brought to more devices and people. For product marketers it may be a bit of a labelling nightmare until all the chargeable devices catch up with the technology: expect MagSafe Compatible (7.5W), MagSafe (15W or 25W), Qi2 15W (15W) and Qi2 25W (25W).
Is Qi2 as fast at wireless charging as MagSafe?
As the Wireless Power Consortium used Apple technology to build the Qi2 specification, it is true that Qi2 matches MagSafe for speed. Both can charge at up to 15W and use the largely same magnetic attachment tech. Note the 25W charging potential of the Apple MagSafe Charger and iPhone 16/17, plus the same charging speed from Qi2 25W.
The first Qi2 charger we tested and reviewed at Macworld was the Anker MagGo 3-in-1 Wireless Charging Station. We tested its Qi2 wireless charging speed by charging an iPhone 15 Pro all the way to a 100% full charge, and taking timings at 30%, 50% and 80%. We did the same using a Apple’s own MagSafe Charger and also via a straight wired USB-C connection.
The fastest way to charge an iPhone is via a wired connection: USB-C to Lightning for iPhones older than the iPhone 15, and USB-C to USB-C for the iPhone 15 and later. The average wired-charging time in our tests was 25 minutes to 50%, 55 minutes to 80% and 70 minutes to 100%.
Our wireless charging tests for officially Apple-certified MagSafe chargers (using Apple’s own Wireless Charger) and for Qi2 magnetic wireless charging (using the Anker MagGo) had remarkably similar timings. There was some variance either way but also small differences using the same charger so we are confident that using these two magentic wireless charging technologies came up with the same basic results on average: 45 minutes to 50%, 90 minutes to 80% and 115 minutes to 100%. 
In summary, then, MagSafe and Qi2 charging at 15W results in the same times and so can be considered equal—except for the 25W MagSafe potential of the iPhone 16/17–and the same from Qi2 25W now it is released. And, again as expected, merely MagSafe-compatible chargers took twice as long as the 15W chargers: 45 minutes to 30%, and 90 minutes to 50%.
Our tests demonstate that Qi2 25W will charges an iPhone 16 Pro from 0–50% in just over 30 minutes—manufacturers often claim 25 minutes but that is under clinical conditions. In Macworld’s real-world tests 32-34 minutes is the average. In comparison, a Qi2 15W charger generally takes about 45 minutes to reach the same level—this would work out as the 25W option being around 45% faster than the 15W chargers. Wireless charging depends on many factors, such as device settings, usage during charging, and ambient temperature.
Don’t concern yourself greatly about the 22W limit of the iPhone 16 and 16 Pro. The 3% difference between that and 25W is marginal.
Why does phone charging speed slow down as the battery gets fuller?
Batteries charge slower the fuller they get, especially in the last 10–20% of charging. The fuller the battery is, the slower it absorbs energy.
To start with, a Lithium-Ion battery accepts whatever current it can, but as the battery gets closer to being full it accepts less current, and so the power being transferred tapers off.
Imagine you were filling up a glass with water. You can start with the faucet or tap at full blast, but as the glass gets fuller, you have to slow the flow down to avoid the water spilling over, until eventually just a trickle of water goes in as you try to get it right up to the brim.
If the battery didn’t charge this way and instead filled up at full blast till reaching 100%, it would get very hot and you’d risk damaging it to the point it might explode!
Slowing down the charge when the battery is getting closer to full also increases the number of charge cycles a battery can go through before it permanently loses capacity.
Taking advantage of this, if you need to charge quickly, stop at 80%, use the device for a while and then top back up to 80% before the charging speed starts to slow.
